title: Set and lock a robot gripper opening stop, then verify retained motion
objective: On an unpressurized, already-assembled representative SCHUNK DRG 80 bench fixture, adjust the opening-stop screw to a declared 90° total opening, lock it without changing the setting, withdraw both tools, and operate a cold test lever to verify retained opening over repeated cycles.
skills: open-ended wrench seating on a thin jam nut
coupled screw adjustment and nut locking
success_conditions: Initial score is 0. Award 0.25 for a released opening within 6° of the declared 90° target; 0.5 when within 3° with nut 73 seated against the cover and nut 74 retained in its modeled installed position; 0.75 when both tools are removed and one close-open cycle returns within 3°; 1.0 after three cycles each return within 3°, stop drift is at most 2°, both nuts remain retained, and tools and robot grippers remain at least 30 mm clear for one second. Revoke angle and cycle credit whenever locking, retention, or clearance prerequisites fail. A missing screw or nut, a dropped or inaccessible tool, fixture displacement, non-finite state, or a configured maximum-opening setting outside the modeled 20°–180° adjustment range, or a violation of the fixture's actual mechanical limits, scores 0. Ordinary closing below 20° during functional cycles is permitted. Equivalent safe strategies earn the same outcome score; arm identity, order, path, action count, and impulse windows are not graded. The target, tolerances, cycle count, and clearance are explicit benchmark assumptions checkable by protractor, witness marks, nut-gap inspection, and video.
industrial_value: SCHUNK specifies opening-angle adjustment, locking, and pneumatic functional testing for its DRG 44–80 industrial grippers, making this direct robot-end-effector setup work within Impact on AI timelines. Its tested ability differs from generic tightening and the accepted hose-clamp task: the robot must preserve an adjustable stop against locknut reaction and then demonstrate hands-off functional retention. It also differs from PR 1540 because two concentric tools act on a coupled screw-and-nut setting rather than stabilizing a sensor body during connector assembly, and from PR 2229 because no third-body feeler gauge or cam clamp establishes the target.
dexterity: One gripper must keep a driver seated in the adjustment screw while the other seats and turns a wrench on nut 73. Tightening must physically tend to disturb an unrestrained screw, requiring coordinated countertorque, angular regulation, possible wrench regrasping, clean tool withdrawal, and subsequent operation of the articulated test fixture.

asset_plan: Build independently authored, full-scale representative rigid geometry, not a redistributed SCHUNK CAD model. Preserve the catalog drawing’s dimensional semantics: 100 × 71.6 × 135.5 mm are catalog X/Y/Z reference dimensions, not a claimed bounding envelope, and the page-7 drawing separately shows a 183.35 mm extent to point P. Represent the anodized-aluminum housing, steel angular jaws, native revolute jaw joints, common centric coupling, accessible adjustment screw, nut 73 as the locking nut, and retained nut 74 as the second manufacturer-specified nut; its precise spacing and role beyond installation are disclosed fixture assumptions because the manual does not explain them. Provide real hex and wrench contact geometry and a native or conservative task-local torque/friction mechanism in which tightening disturbs an unrestrained screw. The cold lever replaces pneumatic actuation only for bench verification. Target angle, hardware dimensions absent from the manual, friction, preload, and tolerances remain declared assumptions. Before demo development, validate reset, tool seating, restrained-versus-unrestrained causality, joint traces, loss cases, release clearance, and timestep sensitivity in the pinned Isaac Sim 6.1/YAM runtime.
risk: Closest ability-level neighbors include PR 1540, PR 1799, PR 1865, PR 2018, PR 2167, and PR 2229. Novelty depends on retaining genuine concentric two-tool screw/nut countertorque and functional-cycle verification; an implementation with zero driver reaction or a scripted phase flag would collapse into existing stabilization or adjustment tasks. No current native gripper trial exists, so implementation feasibility and physics validation remain future gates rather than claimed evidence.
